title: The CPU: Fetch, Decode, Execute
summary: A CPU repeats one cycle billions of times a second - fetch the instruction its program counter points at, decode what it means, execute it, and move on. A tiny computer with one register and seven instructions shows the whole idea, including how a loop is just a jump back.
markdown:
## The parts of a CPU A CPU has three main parts: | Part | Job | |---|---| | **Registers** | A few fast storage slots (4.03). One special register, the **program counter** (PC), holds the address of the next instruction | | **ALU** | Does the arithmetic and logic (4.02) | | **Control unit** | Reads each instruction and switches the right circuits on to carry it out | A **clock** ticks billions of times a second (that is the "GHz" in 1.05), and on each tick the CPU moves one step forward. ## The cycle Everything a CPU does is this loop, forever: ```mermaid flowchart LR F["Fetch
read the instruction
at the address in the PC"] --> D["Decode
work out what it means"] --> E["Execute
do it: add, copy,
jump..."] --> N["Move the PC on
(unless the instruction
jumped)"] --> F ``` 1. **Fetch**: read the instruction stored at the address in the program counter. 2. **Decode**: split it into its parts - which operation, which register, which address. 3. **Execute**: do it, using the ALU, registers and memory. 4. **Next**: add one to the program counter (the size of the instruction), so the next fetch gets the next instruction. ## A tiny computer Here is a complete computer, small enough to watch. It has 16 memory cells, holding both the program and the data (the stored-program idea from 1.03), one register **A** (the accumulator), and seven instructions. Each instruction is a number: the hundreds digit is the operation, the rest is a memory address. | Code | Instruction | Does | |---|---|---| | 1xx | `LOAD xx` | A = the number in cell xx | | 2xx | `ADD xx` | A = A + the number in cell xx | | 3xx | `SUB xx` | A = A − the number in cell xx | | 4xx | `STORE xx` | the number in cell xx = A | | 5xx | `JUMP xx` | the PC = xx: the next instruction comes from cell xx | | 6xx | `JUMPZ xx` | if A is 0, the PC = xx; otherwise carry on | | 000 | `HALT` | stop | So the number `110` means "LOAD 10", and `412` means "STORE 12". ```demo-cpu program: add ``` Press **Step** in the demo and watch: the PC picks the cell, the instruction is fetched into the instruction register, decoded, and executed. This program loads 7, adds 5, and stores 12 in cell 12, in four instructions. Change the numbers in cells 10 and 11 and run it again. ## Loops are jumps back There is no "repeat" instruction. A loop is just a **jump** to an earlier address, and stopping the loop is a **conditional jump** that skips out when something becomes zero: ```demo-cpu program: countdown ``` | Cell | Code | Instruction | Meaning | |---|---|---|---| | 0 | 110 | LOAD 10 | A = the counter | | 1 | 605 | JUMPZ 5 | if A is 0, jump to 5 (the end) | | 2 | 311 | SUB 11 | A = A − 1 | | 3 | 410 | STORE 10 | save the counter | | 4 | 501 | JUMP 1 | go back to the test | | 5 | 000 | HALT | stop | Every `while` loop, `for` loop and `if` in every language becomes jumps like these. The third demo program, `multiply`, multiplies by adding in a loop: ```demo-cpu program: multiply ``` ## Real CPUs A real CPU follows the same cycle, with refinements that make it fast: - **Many registers** (x86-64 has 16 general ones, each 64 bits) instead of one. - **Hundreds of instructions**, including multiply, divide, floating point, and instructions that work on several numbers at once. - **Pipelining**: while one instruction executes, the next is being decoded and the one after is being fetched, like an assembly line. - **Several instructions at once**: modern cores look ahead and run independent instructions side by side, often 4 to 8 per tick. - **Branch prediction**: before a conditional jump is decided, the CPU guesses which way it will go and starts on that path, undoing the work if it guessed wrong. But it is still fetch, decode, execute. In this milestone's project you will build the tiny computer above in Python, and in the next milestone, an assembler for it. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does the program counter hold? - The result of the last sum + The address of the next instruction to fetch - The number of instructions run so far > It is the CPU's bookmark in the program. ? In the tiny computer, what does the number 412 mean? - Add 412 to A + STORE 12: copy A into cell 12 - Jump to cell 12 > The hundreds digit (4) is the operation; 12 is the address. ? How is a loop made in machine code? - With a special REPEAT instruction + With jumps: back to repeat, and out to stop - The CPU repeats the whole program > JUMP goes back to an earlier instruction; a conditional jump such as JUMPZ leaves when the counter reaches zero. ? Why can the tiny computer's program be changed by changing numbers in memory? - It has a built-in program editor - It cannot be changed at all + The program is numbers in the same memory > The program is stored in the same memory as the data: the stored-program design of 1.03. ```

cards.q: What does the program counter hold?
cards.a:
The address of the next instruction to fetch

It is the CPU's bookmark in the program.

cards.q: In the tiny computer, what does the number 412 mean?
cards.a:
STORE 12: copy A into cell 12

The hundreds digit (4) is the operation; 12 is the address.

cards.q: How is a loop made in machine code?
cards.a:
With jumps: back to repeat, and out to stop

JUMP goes back to an earlier instruction; a conditional jump such as JUMPZ leaves when the counter reaches zero.

cards.q: Why can the tiny computer's program be changed by changing numbers in memory?
cards.a:
The program is numbers in the same memory

The program is stored in the same memory as the data: the stored-program design of 1.03.
